opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the physical world doesn't respect the resolution you happen to have. Many of the phenomena we care about most are multi-scale. Take weather and climate. The big atmospheric patterns are thousands of kilometers across, but what actually drives them includes cloud formation, convection, and turbulence that happen at meters or less. If your model only sees coarse grids, those small-scale processes get averaged away, and you have to patch them back in with hand-tuned parameterizations. That's exactly where a lot of the error and uncertainty in traditional models comes from.

The same is true in fluid dynamics, materials, and plasma physics. Turbulence is the classic example. Energy cascades across scales, so small eddies feed back into large-scale behavior. If you never resolve that fine structure, you're not really learning the physics. You're learning a blurred approximation of it, and that approximation tends to break down exactly when you need it, in extreme events or in new regimes outside the training data.

This is also why I think standard deep learning architectures fall short here. A typical neural network is tied to a fixed grid or a fixed pixel resolution. That's fine for images on the internet, but physical fields are really continuous functions. That's the motivation behind neural operators. They learn mappings between function spaces, so you can train on data at different resolutions, combine coarse and fine data, and then evaluate at whatever resolution you need, including zero-shot super-resolution. You're learning the underlying operator, not memorizing a particular discretization.

There's also a practical reason. High-resolution simulation with traditional numerical solvers is enormously expensive. Resolving all the relevant scales can take supercomputers weeks. If AI is going to deliver the speedups we've seen, often thousands to hundreds of thousands of times faster, then it has to be faithful at the fine scales too. Otherwise you get speed at the cost of the very details that matter, like where a hurricane makes landfall or whether a design will fail under stress.

Finally, high-resolution data, combined with physics constraints, is what gives you generalization. Language models can lean on internet-scale text. In science we often have limited data, but if it's rich in fine-scale structure and you enforce the governing equations, the model can extrapolate in ways that are physically consistent. To me that's the path from AI that interpolates to AI that can actually be trusted for scientific discovery and engineering design.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the physics lives at the fine scales. If you think about something like weather, or turbulence in a fluid, or the way a hurricane intensifies, the phenomena that actually determine the outcome are happening at resolutions far below what traditional simulations can afford to compute. Classical numerical solvers have to discretize space and time, and the cost blows up as you refine that grid. So for decades we've been forced to approximate the small-scale physics with hand-crafted parameterizations, and those approximations are exactly where the errors creep in.

What we found with neural operators, going back to our work on the Fourier Neural Operator, is that you can learn the solution operator itself, the mapping from input conditions to output fields, in a way that is resolution-invariant. You can train on one resolution and evaluate at another, and you can actually do zero-shot super-resolution. But the model is only as good as the physics it has seen. If you train only on coarse data, you've baked in the same smoothing that limits the classical solvers. If you have access to high-resolution data, whether from fine-scale simulations or from satellite and sensor observations, the model can learn those multi-scale interactions directly, and that's what gives you both the speed and the fidelity.

The other piece is that high resolution is what makes these models useful for real decisions. With FourCastNet, for example, we're running tens of thousands of times faster than numerical weather prediction, which means you can generate huge ensembles and actually quantify the probability of an extreme event, like where a hurricane makes landfall. That matters enormously for people on the ground, but only if the resolution is fine enough to capture the local features, the coastlines, the terrain, the sharp gradients where the damage actually happens. Coarse models wash those out.

And I'd say this generalizes beyond weather. In medical devices, in aerodynamics, in materials, the whole promise of AI for science is that we can simulate and design in ways that were computationally impossible before. But simulation that misses the fine-scale physics is just a fast way to be wrong. So high-resolution data isn't a nice-to-have for us, it's the foundation.

astra-6.text:
Because in the physical world, small-scale details can have a big impact on what happens at larger scales. Think about turbulence: if your resolution is too coarse, you miss the small eddies and interactions that influence the overall flow. So resolution isn’t just about making an image look sharper. It’s about capturing the physics that determines how a system evolves.

At the same time, high resolution makes traditional simulation very expensive. That’s an important opportunity for AI: can we learn from detailed simulations and observations, then predict how these systems evolve much faster? The challenge is to preserve those interactions across scales, rather than produce something that looks plausible but gets the underlying dynamics wrong.

sol-6.1.text:
When you’re simulating the physical world, the details at small scales can influence what happens at large scales. Think about weather: clouds, turbulence, and local changes in temperature or moisture all affect how a storm develops. If your data is too coarse, you average away some of the very dynamics you want the model to learn.

So high resolution isn’t just about producing a sharper picture. It’s about capturing the interactions that govern how a physical system evolves. The challenge is to learn those dynamics efficiently, so we can make predictions that are both fast and faithful to the underlying physics.
